title: Docker & Containerization Mastery Test
description: Test your Docker proficiency: Dockerfile directives, image layers, volumes, bridge networks, and Docker Compose.

questions.question: What is the difference between `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` in a Dockerfile?
options: `ENTRYPOINT` sets the default executable command; `CMD` provides default arguments that can be overridden easily by CLI parameters
`CMD` executes during docker build; `ENTRYPOINT` executes at runtime
`ENTRYPOINT` can only run Python scripts
There is no functional difference
questions.explanation: `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]` defines the fixed container binary, while `CMD ["--port", "8080"]` defines default parameters that can be overridden at run time.

questions.question: Why should you order Dockerfile instructions from least frequently changing to most frequently changing?
options: To maximize Docker layer caching and significantly reduce container image build times
Because Docker throws an error if commands are out of order
To compress image layers onto disk
To ensure network ports open in sequential order
questions.explanation: Docker invalidates cache for all downstream instructions whenever a layer changes. Placing dependency installation (e.g. `npm install`) before source code copying preserves build cache.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker Named Volume and a Bind Mount?
options: Named Volumes are managed directly by Docker inside `/var/lib/docker/volumes`; Bind Mounts map an exact host directory path into the container
Bind Mounts persist data when containers are deleted while Named Volumes do not
Named Volumes only work on Windows hosts
Bind Mounts can only be read-only
questions.explanation: Named volumes are isolated and managed by Docker for database persistence; bind mounts link specific workstation host directories for live code development.

questions.question: What command removes all stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images in one step?
options: docker system prune
docker clean --all
docker destroy
docker reset
questions.explanation: `docker system prune` frees disk space by deleting stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and build caches.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `.dockerignore` file?
options: Excludes files and directories (like `node_modules`, `.git`, secrets) from the build context sent to the Docker daemon
Prevents Docker from installing Linux security updates
Ignores runtime errors inside the container
Hides containers from `docker ps` commands
questions.explanation: `.dockerignore` prevents transferring heavy local files (`.git`, `node_modules`, `.env`) into the build context, accelerating build times.

questions.question: What is the default network driver assigned to standalone containers launched with `docker run`?
options: bridge
host
overlay
macvlan
questions.explanation: The default `bridge` network provides private internal IP addresses and port forwarding to the host.

questions.question: What happens when a container reaches its assigned memory limit (`--memory=512m`) and attempts to allocate more RAM?
options: The Linux Out-Of-Memory (OOM) Killer terminates the container process with exit code 137
Docker expands the RAM allocation dynamically from the host
The container pauses until RAM is freed
The container deletes cached files automatically
questions.explanation: When cgroup memory limits are exceeded, the kernel OOM killer kills the primary process in the container (SIGKILL, exit 137).

questions.question: In Docker Compose, what does the `depends_on` attribute control?
options: The startup and shutdown ordering of services (e.g. starting database before API)
The CPU share allocated between services
The Git branch dependencies for build
The network bandwidth throttling
questions.explanation: `depends_on` defines the sequence in which Compose creates and starts services, though application-level readiness health checks should still be used.

questions.question: Why should rootless containers or non-root `USER` directives be used in production Dockerfiles?
options: To mitigate container escape vulnerabilities and prevent attackers from gaining root access to the host kernel
To reduce container disk footprint
To allow containers to run without an operating system
To improve network latency
questions.explanation: Running as a non-root user (e.g. `USER appuser`) adheres to least privilege principles, limiting damage if the application inside is exploited.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Docker Health Checks (`HEALTHCHECK`) in a Dockerfile?
options: Tells Docker how to test if the internal application is actually functional and healthy (not just running the PID)
Scans source code for security vulnerabilities
Monitors physical CPU temperature
Checks if newer Docker image versions are available
questions.explanation: HEALTHCHECK runs commands inside the container (e.g. `curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1`) to signal unhealthy states to orchestrators.
